Technical Writing and Evidence: Course Syllabus
This course develops the ability to produce technical documents that are clear, precise,
and grounded in verifiable evidence. Over 12 weeks, students attend 24 sessions
totaling 48 teaching hours, engaging with real-world writing tasks and evidence
evaluation. The syllabus outlines learning outcomes, assessment methods, and weekly
topics, with a focus on practical skills for professional contexts. All materials and
activities are designed to foster critical thinking and ethical reporting.

1 Course Overview and Learning Outcomes
Table 1: Grading scale and corresponding performance descriptors
The course provides a comprehensive introduction to technical writing principles and
evidence-based practices. Students will learn to craft various technical documents, from
reports to proposals, while integrating credible evidence. Emphasis is placed on clarity,
audience analysis, and ethical standards. By the end, students should be able to plan,
draft, and revise technical texts that meet professional requirements and withstand
scrutiny.
1.1 Module Structure and Sequencing
The course is organized into sequential modules that build upon each other. Starting
with foundational concepts, students progress to complex document types and evidence
synthesis. Each module includes readings, exercises, and discussions that reinforce
learning. The sequencing ensures that students develop skills incrementally, with ample
opportunity to apply feedback and refine their work before advancing to more
challenging assignments.
1.1.1 Core Module: Evidence Gathering and Evaluation
This module focuses on identifying, collecting, and assessing evidence from various
sources. Students learn to distinguish between primary and secondary sources, evaluate
credibility, and avoid bias. Practical activities include source audits and evidence

mapping. The module emphasizes the importance of transparency in citing evidence and
the consequences of misrepresentation, preparing students for rigorous technical writing
tasks.

1.1.1.1 Source Credibility and Bias Assessment
Students examine criteria for evaluating source credibility, including authority, accuracy,
and currency. They practice assessing bias in both obvious and subtle forms, using
checklists and peer review. Case studies illustrate how biased sources can distort
technical conclusions. The goal is to equip students with systematic methods for vetting
evidence before incorporation into their writing, ensuring that their documents reflect
balanced and reliable information.
1.1.1.2 Data Collection and Documentation Standards
This section covers best practices for collecting and documenting data in technical
contexts. Students learn to design simple data collection instruments, maintain
meticulous records, and adhere to documentation standards that facilitate
reproducibility. Emphasis is placed on ethical considerations, such as informed consent
and data privacy, and on the importance of clear metadata to support evidence integrity
throughout the writing process.
1.1.2 Applied Module: Technical Document Drafting
In this applied module, students draft a variety of technical documents, including
memos, reports, and instructions. They apply evidence evaluation skills to select and
integrate appropriate sources. Peer review and instructor feedback guide revisions. The
module culminates in a portfolio of drafts that demonstrate growth in clarity,
organization, and evidence use, preparing students for professional writing demands.
1.2 Module Assessment and Feedback
Assessment in the module structure is continuous and formative. Students receive
feedback on exercises and drafts through peer review and instructor comments.
Summative assessments include a midterm evidence evaluation project and a final
document portfolio. Feedback is aligned with learning outcomes and emphasizes
actionable improvements. The assessment strategy ensures that students can

demonstrate mastery of both writing and evidence skills by course end.
2 Assessment and Grading Policies
Assessment comprises several components designed to measure both theoretical
understanding and practical application. Grades are based on participation,
assignments, a midterm project, and a final portfolio. Clear rubrics are provided for each
task, detailing expectations for evidence use, clarity, and accuracy. Late submissions are
penalized unless prior arrangements are made. The policies aim to be fair, transparent,
and supportive of student learning.
2.1 Assignment Types and Deadlines
Students complete a range of assignments, including weekly writing exercises, a source
evaluation report, a technical instructions draft, and a final evidence-based report.
Deadlines are spaced to allow for feedback and revision. The table below outlines key
assignments and their due weeks. Each assignment builds toward the final portfolio,
ensuring steady progress and opportunities to apply feedback.

Figure 1: Key assignments and due weeks
2.1.1 Grading Rubrics and Criteria
Rubrics for each assignment specify criteria such as evidence quality, organization,
clarity, and adherence to conventions. Performance levels are described for each
criterion, enabling students to self-assess and target improvements. Rubrics are
discussed in class and available online. Consistency in grading is maintained through
calibration among instructors and moderation of sample assignments, ensuring that all
students are evaluated fairly.
2.1.1.1 Rubric for Evidence Integration
The evidence integration rubric assesses how well students select, evaluate, and
incorporate evidence. Criteria include relevance, credibility, synthesis, and proper
citation. Each criterion is rated on a scale from emerging to exemplary, with descriptors
clarifying expectations. Students receive this rubric early and use it for self and peer
review, fostering a clear understanding of standards for evidence-based writing.

2.1.1.2 Rubric for Clarity and Precision
This rubric focuses on language use, structure, and audience awareness. Criteria include
conciseness, logical flow, correct terminology, and formatting. Descriptors guide
students in producing documents that are easy to read and understand. The rubric is
applied to all written assignments, and feedback highlights specific areas for
improvement, helping students develop a professional writing style.

2.1.2 Peer Review and Self-Assessment Protocols
Peer review is integral to the course. Students follow structured protocols to provide
constructive feedback on drafts, focusing on evidence use and clarity. Self-assessment
checklists help students reflect on their own work before submission. These protocols
cultivate critical evaluation skills and prepare students for collaborative writing
environments, where giving and receiving feedback is routine.
2.2 Academic Integrity and Submission Guidelines
Academic integrity is paramount. All work must be original, and sources must be
properly cited. Students are required to submit assignments through the designated
platform, which checks for plagiarism. Guidelines for collaboration and use of generative
tools are clearly stated. Violations result in disciplinary action as per institutional policy.
The course emphasizes ethical writing practices and respect for intellectual property.
